readings.title: Walking groups for beginners
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A community walking group advertised a gentle route. New members struggled because experienced walkers set a fast pace. The main obstacle was one pace for people with different abilities. The leader followed the front walkers and did not notice that others had fallen behind. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used timed walks and participant feedback. Organizers checked route length, rest points and how comfortable newcomers felt. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated a slower group increased participation. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced two pace options with clear meeting points. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: welcoming language must match the activity. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in walking groups for beginners, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Using an outdoor exercise space
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A park installed exercise equipment. Adults used it less than expected, although the nearby path was busy. The main obstacle was equipment without simple instructions. Several visitors could not tell how to adjust a machine or whether it suited them. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used observations and advice from qualified instructors. The team asked users where they hesitated and checked safe guidance for each device. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated short demonstrations built confidence. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced clear instructions and scheduled introduction sessions. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: equipment alone does not create access. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in using an outdoor exercise space, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A sports hall after school
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A sports hall offered open sessions for teenagers. Attendance varied because school dismissal times were different across the district. The main obstacle was a fixed start that many students missed. Some young people arrived as the main activity ended and left without joining. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used attendance records by arrival time. Staff compared school schedules and asked participants which start time was realistic. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated a later flexible entry helped more students. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a longer session with short repeating activities. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: participation depends on the fit with daily routines. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in a sports hall after school, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Rest spaces along a fitness route
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A riverside fitness route attracted older walkers. Several people turned back early because benches were concentrated near the start. The main obstacle was rest points unevenly placed along the path. The final stretch had a pleasant view but nowhere convenient to pause. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a route map and conversations with walkers. Planners measured distances between seats and asked where people chose to turn around. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated one additional rest point would extend use. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a bench near the long final stretch. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: small facilities can change who can use a route. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in rest spaces along a fitness route, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A useful plan for wellness and sport participation must take account of the people who will use it. An idea may look complete on paper and still create difficulties during an ordinary week. Organizers therefore tried the community physical activity programme on a small scale and invited comments from users with different schedules. They recorded benefits as well as the time and resources needed to provide them. Some findings supported the original aim, while others suggested that the method should change. The group published both kinds of result instead of presenting the trial as a simple success or failure. This allowed residents to discuss the next step with a clearer understanding of its possible effects.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 关于健康习惯与体育参与的有用方案必须考虑实际使用它的人。一个想法在纸上看似完整，平常使用时却仍可能出现困难。因此，组织者小规模试行该服务，并邀请时间安排不同的使用者提出意见。他们既记录益处，也记录提供这些益处所需的时间和资源。有些发现支持最初目标，另一些则表明方法应当调整。团队同时公布两类结果，而没有把试行简单说成成功或失败。这让居民能更清楚地了解可能的影响，再讨论下一步。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the physical activity team about a community activity related to wellness and sport participation. Explain how different people can participate, what should be recorded, and how the results should be shared.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the community physical activity programme. People have noticed one pace for people with different abilities, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
